summary: An island nation in the South Pacific made up of Upolu, Savai'i and other islands, which became independent from New Zealand in 1962 as the first independent Polynesian country; its traditional culture, the "fa'a Samoa" (the Samoan way), is well preserved.

ranking.name: Congregational Christian Church of Samoa
ranking.description: In 1830 the London Missionary Society missionary John Williams landed on Savai'i and was welcomed by Malietoa Vainu'upo, the most powerful chief of the time, and Christianity soon spread through the villages. This Congregational church became the autonomous "Congregational Christian Church of Samoa" around Samoa's independence in 1962; each village has its own pastor, who together with the chiefly (matai) system forms the core of village life, so it has long been the largest denomination.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Marist missionaries of the Catholic Church came to Samoa in 1845 and founded churches and schools with the support of some chiefly families. Because Samoans often decide their faith collectively by family and village, Catholicism has taken firm root in the villages that accepted it and is noted for its work in education; it is still the second-largest denomination.

ranking.name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
ranking.description: Missionaries of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons) came to Samoa in 1888. The church ran schools and helped believers go to Hawaii and Utah in the United States to study and work, attracting many families to join. In 1983 the church built a temple in the capital, Apia, and Samoa has become one of the countries with the highest proportion of Mormons in the world.

ranking.name: Methodism
ranking.description: Methodism was brought in 1835 by Tongan missionaries; Tonga had by then converted to Christianity under Wesleyan influence, and the kinship and political ties between Tonga and Samoa allowed Methodism to develop in some villages. Although it belongs to the same Protestant family as the Congregational church, the differing routes of their missions created separate village spheres of influence.

ranking.name: Assemblies of God
ranking.description: The Assemblies of God belongs to Pentecostalism, which arrived in Samoa only after the mid-20th century and is characterized by speaking in tongues, faith healing and fervent worship. It has attracted many young people and urban residents, some of them converts from traditional denominations, and at times it also creates friction with the authority of the traditional churches in the villages.

religion.background: Samoans originally worshipped Polynesian gods led by the sky god Tagaloa, as well as ancestral spirits. After the London Missionary Society missionaries arrived in 1830, Christianity spread quickly within a few decades, and village pastors and chiefs jointly govern their communities. During German (1900-1914) and New Zealand (1914-1962) rule, the various denominations continued to develop. In 1962 Samoa became the first independent island nation in the Pacific, and in 2017 a constitutional amendment declared Samoa a Christian state; religion remains central to national identity and village life.

language.official: The official languages are Samoan and English.

ranking.name: Samoan
ranking.description: Samoan belongs to the Polynesian branch of the Austronesian family; in the 19th century London Missionary Society missionaries devised a Latin-alphabet writing system for it, and in the mid-19th century translated the full Bible. Samoan has a set of honorific language used toward chiefs (matai) and pastors, closely tied to the traditional social system. Because the population is almost entirely Samoan and traditional culture is well preserved, the great majority of citizens speak it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: The status of English comes from the period of New Zealand rule, 1914-1962, when English became the language of administration and of education from secondary school upward. After independence English became an official language together with Samoan, widely used in government, law and business. Because large numbers of Samoans have moved to New Zealand, Australia and the United States, English is becoming more and more important in overseas communities, but very few people in Samoa speak it as a mother tongue.

language.history: Samoan is one of the oldest Polynesian languages, gradually taking shape after the Austronesian people of the Lapita culture arrived in Samoa about three thousand years ago. Samoan has two sets of vocabulary, everyday and honorific, reflecting a social structure centered on chiefs. In the 19th century missionaries created a writing system for Samoan, and church schools taught in Samoan, giving it a fairly high literacy rate from early on. English influence grew during the German and New Zealand periods, and today Samoan and English are both official languages.

ranking.name: Palusami
ranking.description: Thick coconut cream with onion and salt is wrapped in young taro leaves, then wrapped again in banana leaves or breadfruit leaves and baked in an earth oven, giving a smooth, rich texture.
ranking.history: Taro and coconut are both crops brought to Samoa by the Austronesian ancestors thousands of years ago, and cooking food wrapped in leaves in an earth oven is also an ancient Polynesian technique. Palusami is an essential dish of the family feast, the "to'ona'i," after the Sunday church service, and often appears at weddings, funerals and chief-title ceremonies. In recent years some families add canned corned beef to the filling, reflecting the influence of imported foods in the 20th century.

ranking.name: Umu (earth oven)
ranking.description: Volcanic stones are heated by fire on the ground, and foods such as taro, breadfruit, pork, fish and palusami are wrapped in leaves, placed on the stones, covered with more leaves and slowly cooked for several hours.
ranking.history: The earth oven is a method of cooking that the Polynesians developed in the era before metal cookware, allowing a large amount of food to be cooked at once. In Samoa, on Sunday morning the men and boys of the household are responsible for lighting the fire and preparing the umu, and after church the whole family and relatives enjoy the meal together, which is regarded as an important part of the "fa'a Samoa." At major festivals and chiefly ceremonies, the amount of food from the earth oven also symbolizes the family's status and generosity.

ranking.name: Koko Samoa (Samoan cocoa)
ranking.description: Roasted cacao beans are pounded into a thick paste of cocoa, which is boiled with hot water and sugar into a rich drink; it can also be cooked with rice or cassava into a sweet porridge.
ranking.history: Cacao originated in the Americas; during the German colonial period of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, German plantation companies planted cacao and coconut on a large scale in Samoa, making cacao an important local crop. Samoans roast and pound the cacao beans themselves into "koko" balls and developed a distinctive way of drinking it. Today Samoan cocoa is a traditional drink for breakfast and when entertaining guests, and also a common souvenir.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: Breadfruit is a large starchy fruit, often roasted whole in an earth oven or over a fire, or boiled or stewed in coconut milk, with a soft, slightly sweet texture.
ranking.history: Breadfruit is one of the crops that the Austronesian ancestors brought when they migrated to the Pacific, and it grows luxuriantly in Samoa's hot, humid climate and is a traditional staple. In the past islanders fermented breadfruit and buried it in pits to cope with food shortages caused by cyclones or poor harvests. Today it still often appears at Sunday earth-oven feasts, served together with taro and palusami.

ranking.name: Sapasui (Samoan chop suey)
ranking.description: Glass noodles stir-cooked with beef or chicken, soy sauce, ginger, garlic and vegetables, with a salty, savory flavor, often appearing at feasts together with white rice.
ranking.history: "Sapasui" is the Samoan pronunciation of the English "chop suey," and it derives from the Chinese laborers recruited from China by the German colonial government to work on plantations from 1903 to 1914. The glass noodle and soy sauce dishes they brought gradually merged into Samoan cuisine, and some of the laborers also settled and started families locally. Today sapasui is an almost indispensable dish at weddings, birthdays and church gatherings, symbolizing the historical link between Samoa and the Chinese.
